events/1295_arte/phases/0/transitionText: At the lectern, Boccaccio closes the Vita Nuova and takes up a volume of city records.
events/1295_arte/phases/0/announcement/t: Boccaccio: “If you want to destroy a poet, first put him into politics. In 1295 he went and signed up with a guild — the guild of doctors and apothecaries. Don't laugh: in those days books were filed with the medicines.”
events/1295_arte/phases/1/narrative: The Ordinances of Justice are in force: the great families may hold no office, and anyone who wants a say in the city must join a guild. Dante, thirty years old, walks in among the medicine drawers and the scales, to sign one piece of paper that will change his life.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/instruction: Sign the register, and listen to Florence's new quarrel while you're there.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/0/dialogu: You know the new Ordinances of Justice? They're aimed at the great families and their bullying — a commoner who wants office has to join a guild.
Entered in the guild of doctors and apothecaries, year's dues paid. Congratulations — you can take part in government now.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/1/dialogu: A poet? You belong to us.
Don't pull that face — spices, medicines, pigments, books: all of them rare goods from far away, all carried in along the same road.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/2/dialogu: A new copy of Virgil, come up from Bologna. Want it? I'll give you a good price.
More people can read now. Florence's arithmetic schools are busier than the monasteries. Books are good business.
events/1295_arte/phases/1/npcs/3/dialogu: Lord Corso of the Donati was out in the square shouting at people again this morning — his lot are called the Blacks now.
The Cerchi made their money in trade — rich, new money. Their lot are called the Whites. Both of them Guelphs, and they go at each other like dogs.
The Ghibellines — the emperor's side? Driven out of the city long ago. The whole city is Guelph now, the pope's side. No enemy left outside, so they fight their own.
events/1295_arte/phases/2/narrative: The paperwork is done. On the Ponte Vecchio in the last light, the others are waiting for him.
events/1295_arte/phases/2/instruction: Talk to your friends on the bridge, then listen to your own heart.
events/1295_arte/phases/2/npcs/0/dialogu: Politics is mud, Durante. You and I write poems.
(The Guido saying this is himself a leading man of the Whites.)
events/1295_arte/phases/2/npcs/1/dialogu: Well now, “my lord”! A great man of the apothecaries' guild! Do I get a discount on my medicine from here on?
We'll trade a few more sonnets soon — I still owe you an answer for that last one you wrote at me.
(Forese is Corso's younger brother, and Dante's drinking companion. The two of them wrote rude poems at each other, every line drawing blood — and the friendship was real too.)
events/1295_arte/phases/2/npcs/2/dialogu: Guido says politics is mud. And yet—
A city should have order, the way a poem does. I'm going to go and write that order into it.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/lede:
You are the head of one Florentine family. The family across from you is not of your party.
Every time the city changes hands, whoever is in power has to decide: drive the other side out, or let them stay.
The ones you drive out do not disappear — they wait in another city, waiting to come back with outside help.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/0: In 1300 Dante signed a list of men to be banished. His best friend's name was on it.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/1: When he signed it he believed this: hold both parties to the same rule, and the city will settle down.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/2: In 1302 that same rule drove him out.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/3: In 1315 Florence said: pay the fine, put on the penitent's robe, walk through the streets to the Baptistery, and you can come home. He refused.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/4: What was wrong with Florence was never that one side was worse than the other. It was that the city turned “exile” into a move you could play over and over —
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/lines/5: the loser can always come back with outside help, and the winner knows it, so each time he strikes harder.
events/1295_arte/phases/3/coda/turn:
Then he wrote the Inferno.
A world with only one round: once the sentence is given it never changes, there is no next move, no way back.

And the lowest level of Hell is not for killing, not for violence —
it is for betrayal. For the people who destroy trust.
That level is frozen: down there, nothing will ever change again.
events/1295_arte/phases/4/transitionText: A different voice takes the lectern — Pietro Alighieri, Dante's son, one of the first men to write a commentary on the Divine Comedy.
events/1295_arte/phases/4/announcement/t: Echoes down the years · Pietro's commentary

“My father believed a city could be governed by reason. Later, in Inferno VI, he has Ciacco the glutton foretell how this city would tear itself apart — the two parties at each other, blood in the streets. That prophecy is really a memory. And through Ciacco's mouth he names the disease: pride, envy and greed are the three sparks that set every heart burning.”
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/0/question: In 1295, which guild did Dante join in order to take part in government?
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/0/options/0: The guild of doctors and apothecaries
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/0/explanation: Under the Ordinances of Justice, you had to belong to a guild to take part in government. Books were classed with medicines then, and booksellers hung on to the apothecaries' guild — so the poet signed up with the doctors and apothecaries.
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/1/question: In the 1290s the Guelphs of Florence split into the Whites and the Blacks. Which family led each?
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/1/explanation: The Whites were led by the Cerchi, new money grown rich in trade; the Blacks by Corso of the Donati, an old noble house. Both were Guelphs, and they fought each other to the death — Dante's family were Whites.
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/2/question:
Inferno VI: Ciacco foretells how Florence will tear itself apart.
“Pride, envy and greed are the three ___ that set every heart burning”
quiz/1295_arte/quizzes/2/explanation: Inferno VI: Ciacco foretells to Dante that the two parties will fight and the Whites will be driven out — and he names the disease: “pride, envy and greed are the three sparks that set every heart burning.”
